headline: Constellation Energy: EPS of $5.06 beats by 30% and guidance rises again as Google and Amazon sign up for nuclear power; shares up 10%
takeaway: Adjusted operating earnings rose to $5.06 a share from $3.04, about 30% above the $3.89 consensus, helped by the Calpine acquisition and strong power markets. Constellation raised the midpoint of its full-year guidance to $12.50–$12.80, announced 20-year contracts with Google and Amazon, and the shares jumped 10%.
results: Constellation Energy reported GAAP net income of $5.19 a share for the third quarter, up from $2.97, and adjusted operating earnings of $5.06, up from $3.04 and well ahead of analysts’ $3.89. The company attributed the increase to favourable market and portfolio conditions and the addition of Calpine, bought in January, partly offset by higher interest costs and a smaller benefit from the federal nuclear production tax credit. Revenue was about $9.6 billion.

The nuclear fleet produced 46,677 gigawatt-hours, slightly more than a year earlier, and plants excluding the Salem and South Texas joint ventures ran at a 97.2% capacity factor, up from 96.8%. With Calpine’s gas fleet now included, the company has begun reporting forced-outage rates for its gas, oil and renewable plants as a key operating measure.

Constellation agreed to buy the 609-megawatt Rhode Island State Energy Center, a gas-fired plant, from Shell for $715 million, and signed a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion from the Department of Energy to fund nuclear uprates.
mgmt: Chief executive Joe Dominguez said the quarter’s agreements add more than 1,000 megawatts of new emissions-free capacity — the equivalent of a large nuclear plant — with no cost to existing customers. The largest are a 20-year power purchase agreement with Google supporting $4.3 billion of investment to add about 890 megawatts across 11 nuclear units, plus a 15-year, 2,700-megawatt load-following agreement; and a 20-year, 690-megawatt agreement with Amazon supporting more than $3 billion of investment at Calvert Cliffs, including a 190-megawatt expansion due between 2030 and 2032.

Chief financial officer Shane Smith said the results allowed the company to raise the midpoint of its guidance for the second time this year, to $12.50–$12.80 a share, and pointed to uprates, the Rhode Island purchase and an aggressive pace of share repurchases as drivers of sustained earnings growth. The company also launched Peak+, a product combining new capacity and energy supply for large customers, with a first 20-year, 270-megawatt contract.
view: Constellation has become the market’s cleanest way to own the idea that artificial intelligence needs reliable, carbon-free power around the clock, and this quarter supplied the proof that the idea pays. A 30% earnings beat is large for a power company, and it came from the merchant side of the business — selling power and capacity at market prices that have risen sharply in the PJM grid as data-centre demand outruns new supply. That is the part of the story investors had doubted: whether the high prices of 2025 would last.

The contracts matter more than the quarter. The Google and Amazon deals do something different from last year’s headline restart agreements: they pay for uprates and expansions at existing plants — about 1,080 megawatts in total — that are cheaper and faster to build than new reactors, and they lock in 20 years of revenue from the most creditworthy buyers in the world. Combined with a DOE loan of up to $5 billion at government rates, Constellation is effectively being paid to grow its fleet by its customers and financed by the state.

The risks are political and financial rather than operational. Regulators in PJM are under pressure over rising consumer bills, and any cap on capacity prices or rules forcing data centres to bring their own generation would hit the merchant earnings that drove this beat. The company is also more leveraged after the $26 billion-plus Calpine deal, and it now owns a large gas fleet whose value depends on gas and power spreads. At about 19 times this year’s guided earnings, well above the multiple of a regulated utility, the shares already assume the contracts keep coming. This report gives no reason to doubt that, but it leaves little room for a policy shock.
watch: Watch the next PJM capacity auction and any regulatory action on prices, further hyperscaler contracts, the closing of the Rhode Island acquisition and the 2027 guidance in February.
